claim: /k, h, r/ are restricted to loans in the tautala lelei inventory summarized from Mosel & Hovdhaugen; these parenthesized consonants are typically tied to the literary/formal register.
scope: Alderete & Bradshaw 2012 synopsis of Mosel & Hovdhaugen 1992
exceptions_or_counterexamples: /k/ also occurs in some interjections and borrowings from tautala leaga; /h/ may be used emphatically word-initially when addressing domestic animals.

claim: Oral stops /p t k/ may be voiced intervocalically in fast speech, and may be weakly aspirated under emphasis, around stressed vowels, or utterance-initially.

processes: optional intervocalic voicing in fast speech
weak aspiration in emphatic/prosodically strong contexts

normalized_environment: {p,t,k} -> optionally voiced / V__V in fast speech; weak aspiration under emphasis/near stress/#__
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Aspiration is reported as more common among young people and children, indicating sociophonetic variation rather than a categorical rule.

claim: /t/ has a palatalized/affricated realization before /i/, with the affricated variant described as increasingly common and especially associated with women and children.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The ordinary lamino-alveolar realization remains available; this is variable and socially patterned.

claim: Intervocalic /ʔ/ may be realized as creaky voice and is often dropped between identical vowels in fast speech; word-initial /ʔ/ is highly unstable except in careful speech.

processes: ʔ -> ∅ / V__V when vowels identical in fast speech

normalized_environment: ʔ weakens intervocalically and word-initially under reduced-speech conditions
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Any vowel-initial word may receive a prothetic [ʔ] under emphasis or phrase-initially, making initial presence/absence distributionally unstable.

claim: Native /v/ does not occur before /u/ and occurs only very rarely before /o/.
normalized_environment: *vu; vo strongly underrepresented in native lexicon
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The statement is lexical-stratum specific and should not be extended automatically to recent loans.

claim: Within a single morpheme, different labial consonants are strongly restricted from co-occurring in consecutive syllables; identical consonants are exempt from the general labial co-occurrence restriction.
formal_environment: C_lab V C_lab V within one morpheme
normalized_environment: OCP-LAB across consecutive syllables within morpheme, identity exempt
scope: single-morpheme native lexicon; synopsis points to Mosel & Hovdhaugen 1992:24-25
exceptions_or_counterexamples: /ʔ{m,p}Vf/ and /pVv/ are explicitly reported as counterexamples; several otherwise disfavored sequences occur across morpheme boundaries or in recent loans.

claim: Some apparent consonant co-occurrence gaps involving /n/ and /ŋ/ may be frequency artifacts rather than productive restrictions; /v/ itself is also described as very low-frequency.

examples: ŋVmV absent in TLL but common in TLG
ŋVvV absent in TLL but common in TLG

normalized_environment: low base frequency may mimic OCP/cooccurrence ban
scope: comparison of tautala lelei and tautala leaga distributions
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Register differences reverse some apparent gaps, which argues against treating all non-attestation as phonological impossibility.

claim: Vowel quality and duration are positionally conditioned: unstressed nonfinal /e/ may become very short or schwa-like, unstressed /a/ centralizes, unstressed /u/ may become [w], and unstressed word-initial /i/ may become a semivowel.

processes: e -> very short/[ə]-like in nonfinal unstressed position

exceptions_or_counterexamples: These are tendencies, not categorical neutralizations, and the synopsis distinguishes phonological length from multiple phonetic length categories.

claim: Sentence-final short vowels may be devoiced or silent in fast colloquial speech, creating surface word/syllable-final consonants that are otherwise phonotactically unacceptable; short /i, u/ deletion may leave palatalization or labialization on the preceding consonant.

source_forms.particle_reduction: CVV -> CV possible in fast speech

formal_environment: short V / __# in fast colloquial speech
normalized_environment: surface coda creation by final-vowel elision
exceptions_or_counterexamples: The resulting final consonants are described as phonotactically unacceptable in the careful/native word-structure system, so surface codas must be linked to the elision process rather than treated as ordinary codas.

claim: Identical vowels can contract across morpheme or word boundaries; when stressed, contraction can yield an extra-long vowel, and the process competes with vowel elision when both vowels are short.

source_forms.schema: Vi=Vi or Vi##Vi -> Vː / Vːː when stressed

exceptions_or_counterexamples: Speakers show a tendency to prefer a variant with vowel elision when contraction and elision compete.

claim: The basic Samoan syllable template is (C)V1(V2): onsets are optional, codas are absent in the careful lexical phonology, and both monomoraic and bimoraic syllables occur.
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Fast colloquial final-vowel loss can create surface final consonants, but these are derived exceptions to the canonical template.

claim: VV sequences may be identical vowels or diphthongs; likely tautosyllabic diphthongs are falling-sonority sequences such as /ei eu ai au ou oi/ and more rarely /ui/, whereas other VV sequences are possible but heterosyllabic.
normalized_environment: selected falling-sonority VV = tautosyllabic nucleus; other VV = hiatus
scope: synopsis of grammar and stress evidence
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Across morpheme boundaries, individual vowels remain monomoraic even where the same sequence would be analyzed as a diphthong morpheme-internally; the /ui/ status is explicitly rare/less secure.

claim: Primary stress falls on the final syllable when that syllable contains a bimoraic VV nucleus (long vowel or diphthong); otherwise stress falls on the penultimate syllable.

source_forms.rule: final heavy -> final stress; otherwise penult

normalized_environment: stress = final if σfinal is bimoraic, else penult
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Antepenultimate syllables are very rarely stressed; compounds preserve component stresses with strongest stress on the final word, so larger prosodic domains require separate treatment.

claim: At phrase level, normal spoken Samoan is described as having roughly one accented syllable per phrase; accent typically falls on the last lexical morpheme, the last phrase of an utterance is obligatorily accented, and short CV/V particles cannot receive accent.

accent_rules: one accented syllable per phrase in normal speech

normalized_environment: phrase accent constrained by lexicality and right edge
exceptions_or_counterexamples: Disyllabic grammatical or lexical words can receive accent sporadically before pauses, under hesitation, or emphasis; coordinated/subordinate phrase sequences can be rephrased as one accentual domain.
